title: Unit finale: bits
sub: New problems, a Single Number III trace with negative numbers, a shift trap on a bitboard, and explaining out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match the condition to the technique.
cards/0/pairs/1/0: Product of two word lengths with no common letters (#318)
cards/0/pairs/3/1: XOR of 1..n and the array, then x & −x
cards/0/pairs/4/0: How many bits to flip to turn a into b
cards/1/q: Maximum Product of Word Lengths (LeetCode #318): up to 1000 words of lowercase Latin letters, each up to 1000 long. Find the maximum len(a) · len(b) over pairs of words with no letters in common. How do you test a pair?
cards/1/options/0: Precompute each word’s letter mask; a pair qualifies if (mask[i] & mask[j]) == 0
cards/1/options/1: For each pair build a HashSet<char> of the first word and scan the second
cards/1/options/2: Sort each word’s letters and merge the two strings as in merge sort
cards/1/explain: The mask is the set of letters in one int: m |= 1 << (c - 'a'), O(total length) to prepare. “No common letters” is an empty intersection, (a & b) == 0, O(1) per pair. About 5·10⁵ pairs — instant.
cards/1/wrong/1: Correct, but O(length) per pair: up to 5·10⁵ pairs of 1000 letters is 5·10⁸ operations, plus allocations.
cards/1/wrong/2: Merging is also O(length) per pair. The mask squeezes a word into 26 bits once.
cards/2/q: Number Complement (#476): flip every bit of num ≥ 1 except the leading zeros: 5 = 101₂ → 010₂ = 2. What do you return?
cards/2/options/0: ~num & mask, where mask has 1s in every bit up to and including the highest 1 of num
cards/2/explain: ~num flips all 32 bits, and the leading zeros become 1s — the result is negative. A mask of the k lowest 1s, (1 << k) − 1, where k is the bit length of num, trims the extra: for 5 the mask is 111₂, ~5 & 7 = 2. num ^ mask gives the same answer.
cards/2/wrong/1: ~5 = −6: the leading zeros became 1s too, the sign bit included.
cards/3/task: Step through Single Number III on [10, 3, −6, 3, 9, 9]: the singles are 10 and −6. The rig asks which bit splits them and which group −6 goes to.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: The lowest 1 of −16 is bit 4, with four zeros below it. 16 has only bit 4 set, and x has it too, so the AND gives 16. The sign does not get in the way: x & −x works in two’s complement for any x ≠ 0. 10 = 01010₂ and −6 = …11010₂ really do differ first in bit 4.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Group b: bit 4 does not count for negatives
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: Second pass, low = 16. −6 = …11111010₂ arrives. Which group does it go to?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: −6 has every bit from 3 to 31 set, bit 4 included: −6 & 16 = 16 ≠ 0, so it is group a. The code compares bits, not values: “less than 16” has nothing to do with it. The 3s and 9s land in b in pairs and cancel, leaving 10 there.
cards/4/q: An 8×8 board is stored in a long, cells sq from 0 to 63. After Place(40), Has(40) returns false and Has(8) returns true. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: 1 << sq shifts an int, and an int takes the count modulo 32: 1 << 40 = 1 << 8 = 256, so the piece lands on cell 8. At sq = 31 it is worse: 1 << 31 is a negative int, widening to long copies the sign, and 1s appear in every cell from 31 to 63. It needs 1L << sq.
cards/5/q: Complexity of this unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/5/options/0: Counting Bits via bits[i >> 1] is O(n)
cards/5/options/1: Maximum XOR with prefix sets is O(31·n) time and O(n) memory
cards/5/options/2: The Kernighan loop always takes exactly 32 steps
cards/5/options/3: The sum without a plus on an int takes at most 32 rounds
cards/5/options/4: Divide Two Integers by long division is O(quotient)
cards/5/explain: Counting Bits is one operation per number. Maximum XOR is 31 passes over n prefixes with a HashSet. Kernighan takes a step per 1 bit, not per bit. In the sum the carry moves left every round and leaves bit 31 within 32 rounds. Long division is 32 steps; O(quotient) is the naive subtraction.
cards/6/q: Unity: 2000 units, each with 5 statuses (burning, frozen, stunned…), and every frame you need to check whether a unit is burning and stunned at the same time. What is the sensible choice?
cards/6/options/0: A [Flags] enum field on the unit and the test (s & both) == both, where both = Burning | Stunned
cards/6/options/1: A HashSet<Status> per unit and two Contains calls
cards/6/options/2: s.HasFlag(Status.Burning) && s.HasFlag(Status.Stunned) — the same thing, just more readable
cards/6/explain: All statuses are bits of one int: testing any combination is one AND and one comparison, with no allocations and the data close together in memory. (s & both) == both requires both bits; (s & both) != 0 requires at least one.
cards/6/wrong/1: A HashSet per unit is 2000 heap objects, hashing on every Contains and data scattered in memory. For 5 values it costs many times more than a mask.
cards/6/wrong/2: On .NET Core 2.1+ it really is a single test, but in Unity HasFlag may box the enum — allocations every frame across 2000 units.
cards/7/q: Interview code tests for odd numbers like this: if (x % 2 == 1). Where does the test go wrong?
cards/7/options/2: Nowhere: the remainder of division by 2 is always 0 or 1
cards/7/explain: In C# the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: −3 % 2 = −1, so the test decides −3 is even. Reliable versions are (x & 1) != 0 or x % 2 != 0: in two’s complement the lowest bit of a negative odd number is 1 as well.
cards/7/wrong/1: 0 % 2 = 0 — zero is even, so the test is right.
cards/7/wrong/2: The remainder can be negative: it takes the sign of the dividend.
cards/8/q: You are solving Single Number II (#137, everything three times, one number once) out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/8/items/0: Clarify: every number three times except one; the range is the whole int, negatives included
cards/8/items/1: Brute force: a dictionary of counts — O(n) time, but O(n) memory
cards/8/items/2: Why not XOR: every triple leaves a copy behind
cards/8/items/3: Idea: for each of the 32 bits count how many numbers have it; the remainder modulo 3 is the answer’s bit
cards/8/items/4: Run it: [2, 2, 3, 2] → bit 0: 1 → 1, bit 1: 4 → 1, the answer is 3
cards/8/items/5: Complexity: O(32·n) time, O(1) memory; bit 31 is collected too, so negatives work
cards/8/explain: Right after the brute force it is worth saying why the familiar trick fails — that shows you understand what XOR relies on. Running a small array checks both the modulo-3 count and assembling the answer from bits.
